title: Inside an assembly
sub: Manifest, modules, resources and type forwarding
cards/0/title: An assembly is more than a file
cards/0/body:
In the unit "How .NET code runs" you saw that a .dll holds CIL and metadata. Now something else matters more: an assembly is the unit of deployment and versioning. It has an identity made of four parts: simple name, version, culture and public key.

A type belongs to an assembly. To the CLR, Shop.Order from the Shop assembly and Shop.Order from the Shop.Legacy assembly are two different types, even though the names match.
cards/0/deep:
This explains a famous puzzle: InvalidCastException: Unable to cast object of type 'Shop.Order' to type 'Shop.Order'. It means the same assembly got loaded twice (say, from two paths or into two load contexts): the full type name matches, the type does not. How assemblies end up in different contexts is the topic of the next unit.

PublicKeyToken=null means the assembly has no strong name. Strong names are lesson 3.
cards/1/body:
The manifest is the part of the metadata that describes the assembly as a whole rather than individual types. It is a few tables:

  • Assembly — its own identity: name, version, culture, public key;
  • AssemblyRef — which assemblies it depends on and which versions it expects;
  • ManifestResource — embedded resources;
  • ExportedType — types the assembly hands over to another assembly;
  • File — other files of the assembly (needed by multi-file assemblies).

This is how a manifest looks in a disassembler:
cards/1/deep: The .ver line in .assembly extern is the version the compiler built your code against. It wrote it into AssemblyRef for good: you can rebuild the dependency, but the reference inside Shop.dll stays 9.0.0.0 until you rebuild Shop itself. What the loader does with that number is lesson 2.
cards/2/q: What makes up an assembly identity?
cards/2/options/0: Name, version, culture and public key
cards/2/explain: These four parts are stored in the Assembly table and in every AssemblyRef. File name, path and date are not part of the identity.
cards/2/wrong/2: FileVersion is a resource for Windows Explorer and is not part of the identity. More in lesson 2.
cards/3/body:
A module is one PE file with metadata. An assembly consists of modules, and one of them holds the manifest.

Then. In .NET Framework an assembly could span several files: csc -target:module produced a .netmodule file without a manifest, and the File table of the main module listed the others with their hashes. This let you glue code in different languages into one assembly or download rarely used parts over the network.

Now. Modern .NET does not support multi-file assemblies: one assembly, one module, one file. Single-file publishing is an entirely different mechanism, covered in the next unit.
cards/3/deep: Every module has its own <Module> type in the metadata — it holds global functions and the module initializer ([ModuleInitializer] in C# 9). Metadata is addressed by tokens scoped to a module, so references between modules of one assembly went through a separate ModuleRef table. In modern projects this legacy barely shows up.
cards/4/q: What does every modern .NET assembly have? Select all.
cards/4/options/1: Exactly one module — the file itself
cards/4/explain: Resources are optional. .netmodule files were part of multi-file assemblies in .NET Framework; the modern runtime does not load them.
cards/5/body:
For a file with the EmbeddedResource build action, the compiler puts its bytes right into the PE file and its name into the ManifestResource table. The name is built like this: the project root namespace, the file path with dots, the file name.

You read a resource as a stream, without unpacking it to disk.
cards/5/deep:
.resx files are compiled into binary .resources and embedded the same way; ResourceManager reads them.

Translations go into satellite assemblies: ru/Shop.resources.dll. Such an assembly has culture ru in its identity and contains no code — only resources. ResourceManager looks for the assembly of the current UI culture, then of its parent culture, and finally falls back to the resources in the main assembly.
cards/6/q: Print the names of all embedded resources and open each one
cards/6/explain: Names come from the ManifestResource table; the stream reads the resource bytes from the PE file. GetFiles is about the files of a multi-file assembly and has nothing to do with embedded resources.
cards/7/title: Version 2: a type moves to another assembly
cards/7/body:
In version 2 the Money class moves from Shop.dll to the new Shop.Core.dll. The old app was not rebuilt, and its IL says [Shop]Shop.Money: the CLR looks for the type in Shop, does not find it — TypeLoadException.

The fix is type forwarding. Shop.dll references Shop.Core and declares an attribute. The compiler writes a row into the ExportedType table, and the CLR, failing to find the type in Shop, follows that row.
cards/7/deep:
The whole modern BCL relies on forwarding. Your code is compiled against System.Runtime, but at run time System.Runtime.dll is an almost empty assembly that forwards Object, String and the rest to System.Private.CoreLib. netstandard.dll from the history course works the same way: a facade that on each platform forwards types to wherever they really live.

The opposite attribute, TypeForwardedFrom, is not for the loader but for serializers that stored the old assembly name in their data.
cards/8/q: Money moved from Shop.dll to Shop.Core.dll without TypeForwardedTo. The old App.exe was not rebuilt. What happens?
cards/8/options/0: TypeLoadException once the Money type is needed
cards/8/options/1: It works: the CLR finds the type by name in any loaded assembly
cards/8/options/2: App.exe will not start: a verification error at process start
cards/8/options/3: Money is loaded from an old copy of Shop.dll in a cache
cards/8/explain: A type reference in IL includes the assembly. The CLR looks for Money only in Shop and fails as soon as the JIT compiles a method that needs that type.
cards/8/wrong/1: There is no such "search every assembly": the assembly name is part of the type reference.
cards/9/q: The manifest of Shop.dll version 2. Which line lets old code find Money?
cards/9/explain: .class extern forwarder is a row of the ExportedType table: "look for Shop.Money in Shop.Core". The TypeForwardedTo attribute creates it.
cards/10/title: Reference assemblies: compile against one, run another
cards/10/body:
The compiler needs only signatures, not method bodies. That is what reference assemblies are: the same public types and methods, but with throw null instead of bodies.

Your project is compiled against reference assemblies from the Microsoft.NETCore.App.Ref pack and runs against the real assemblies of the installed runtime. The only link between them is the identity: name and version in AssemblyRef.
cards/10/code:
// what a method looks like in a reference assembly
public static int Parse(string s) => throw null;
cards/10/deep: A reference assembly carries ReferenceAssemblyAttribute, and the runtime refuses to execute it: BadImageFormatException. The SDK builds a reference assembly for your own projects too (obj/…/ref/): if the public API did not change, dependent projects are not recompiled. That is where fast incremental builds in large solutions come from.
